The first time I noticed how language bends the world, it wasn’t in a classroom or a book. It was in a kitchen, on a gray afternoon that refused to commit to rain. Someone opened a cupboard and said, with mild irritation, “It’s never where it should be.” Nothing dramatic happened after that—no lightning, no revelation. But the sentence changed the room. Suddenly the cupboard wasn’t merely a container of cups and utensils; it became a place governed by rules that could not be satisfied. We were no longer looking for a thing. We were wrestling with fate, with the stubborn refusal of reality to arrange itself according to human expectations.

That’s one way to understand writing: as an act of attention that insists the world is not only happening, but also meaning something. If I had to describe my own relationship to words, I’d say they are less like tools and more like weather. They move in, they shift, they change the temperature of thought. A certain phrasing can make a memory feel sharper, or softer, or altogether different—as if it were never the same event twice.

I’ve always been drawn to the edges of language, where meanings overlap and sometimes betray each other. Take a simple word like “near.” Near to what? Near by distance, time, feeling? Near enough to touch? Near enough to lose? The word seems harmless until you try to use it honestly. Then it starts to behave like a riddle.

When I write, I often start from a single word I can’t stop thinking about. Sometimes it’s a word someone said years ago, something ordinary that unexpectedly carries weight. Other times it’s a word I stumble across in a poem or on a street sign, and it feels like a door I haven’t unlocked yet. I don’t choose these words so much as they choose me. The blank page becomes a kind of shoreline, and the words come in like tidewater—at first tentative, then with a steadiness that makes me suspect they’ve been waiting for the right conditions.

There’s a myth that writing is a straight path from thought to sentence. I don’t believe that. For me, writing is more like navigating a dim room with only occasional flickers of light. I draft and redraft, and what I call “progress” is often just me learning where I’m lost. A sentence works one day and collapses the next. A metaphor that once felt inevitable suddenly feels borrowed or clumsy. Sometimes I find myself rereading a paragraph and realizing it’s not describing the thing I meant to describe at all. It’s describing my attempt to control the thing. That attempt can be the subject of the work even when I didn’t intend it.

If I’m honest, writing also carries a moral dimension. Not morality in the sense of “be good,” but morality in the sense of “be accountable.” When you put words on the page, you are choosing how to represent reality. You are deciding what to emphasize, what to omit, what to frame as important. Even when you’re writing fiction, you are still making a claim about how people behave, how the world works, what counts as cause and effect. That claim can be gentle. It can be cruel. It can be accidental. But it’s still a claim, and it still matters.

I used to think the best writing was the kind that disappeared. You read and you forgot the mechanism behind the words; you fell into the story as if it were a river. Now I suspect that disappearing is not always the goal. Sometimes the visibility of language—the fact that you can see the seams—makes the experience more truthful. If the narrator is uncertain, maybe the prose should show that uncertainty. If a character is lying, maybe the sentences should feel crooked. If the world is changing too quickly to be understood, maybe the writing should feel like it’s changing with it.

This is why I’m drawn to the strange, in-between forms of expression. Essays that act like stories. Stories that pause to consider their own methods. Poems that contain a biography and refuse to list the dates. I love when the work admits it is made, not merely found. The admission doesn’t make the writing weaker; it makes it more human. Humans don’t experience life like a polished artifact. We experience it like a rough draft with interruptions: a thought in one room, a feeling in another, a sudden noise at the edge of hearing that changes everything.

What writing ultimately offers, if it offers anything at all, is the chance to reconsider what you already believe. That reconsideration can be subtle, like moving a chair two inches and noticing that suddenly the light falls differently. Or it can be dramatic, like realizing you’ve been wrong about your own motives for years. Either way, writing becomes a method of self-interrogation. You ask what you mean, and the page answers back with its own stubbornness. There are things you can only discover by trying to express them.

Sometimes the act of writing feels less like construction and more like listening. I sit down and stare at the cursor blinking at me, as if it’s breathing. At first my mind produces noise: mundane anxieties, unfinished errands, small regrets. Then, slowly, the mind begins to settle into the rhythm of attention. Words arrive that I didn’t know I was searching for. They come not as inspiration from above, but as recognition from within. The sentence that finally works isn’t one I invented so much as one I uncovered.

There are also days when nothing arrives. Those are the days I’m tempted to treat writing as a performance—something I should be good at, something I should control. When the page stays empty, I start to bargain with myself: tomorrow, after I’ve fixed my life; tomorrow, after I’ve read more; tomorrow, after I’ve become the kind of person who can effortlessly pour meaning into paragraphs. But “tomorrow” is always a clever disguise for fear.

I’ve learned that writing isn’t a constant surge. It’s mostly return. Return to the sentence. Return to the scene. Return to the breath between drafts. Even when you don’t feel inspired, you can still practice attention. You can still let the work ask questions. You can still show up and admit, with humility, that you don’t know yet what you’re doing.

Over time, the blank page becomes less frightening. Not because I become more confident, exactly, but because I become more intimate with the process. I know that confusion can be productive. I know that bad drafts contain clues. I know that a rough metaphor may become a truthful one if I’m patient. And I know that even when the writing fails to become what I hoped, it has still changed something: my memory, my perspective, my ability to notice.

This is what I mean when I say words are weather. They don’t just describe the world; they reshape it from inside. They influence what I pay attention to. They influence what I choose to keep. They influence what I think counts as a beginning or an ending. A sentence can make a day feel like a turning point. A single clause can reveal the difference between love and obsession.

In the end, I write because I want to be precise about what matters. Precision isn’t about perfection. It’s about honesty with an ear for nuance. It’s about letting the world be complicated without forcing it to fit neatly into the first story you tell about it. The cupboard doesn’t have to be governed by fate; maybe it’s just a matter of habit. The sentence “It’s never where it should be” can become “I put it there without thinking,” or “I’m tired,” or “I miss my old routine.” The meaning of the moment changes, and with it, the kind of future we imagine.

So I keep returning to the page. Sometimes the words come easily. Sometimes they resist. But resistance itself is a kind of information. It tells me where I’m avoiding something, where my assumptions are hiding, where my attention needs to widen. Writing is a way of staying awake to the world’s subtle motion.

And maybe that’s the real reason for language’s power: it doesn’t only record life. It helps make life legible, moment by moment, sentence by sentence—until the world feels less like a riddle and more like a conversation I’m finally ready to join.
